Yes, this is a classical theorem in number theory. There are infinitely many primes of the form 4k + 3 (i.e., primes p where p ≡ 3 (mod 4)).

This is proven by a classic proof similar to Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes.

**Proof:**

Assume there are finitely many primes congruent to 3 mod 4: p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ.

Consider N = 4·p₁·p₂·...·pₙ - 1 = 4(p₁·p₂·...·pₙ - 1) + 3.
So N ≡ 3 (mod 4). Since a product of factors all ≡ 1 (mod 4) would itself be ≡ 1 (mod 4), N must have at least one prime factor q ≡ 3 (mod 4). This q can't equal any of the pᵢ, since N leaves remainder -1 when divided by each pᵢ.

So q is a new prime ≡ 3 (mod 4), contradicting our finite list — hence there are infinitely many such primes. This result is also a special case of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions.

## Yes — There Are Infinitely Many Primes ≡ 3 (mod 4)

This is a classical result, provable with an argument similar to Euclid's proof of infinite primes.

---

### Proof by Contradiction

**Assume** there are only finitely many such primes: $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$, all satisfying $p_i \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.

**Construct** the number:
$$N = 4p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k - 1$$

Note that $N \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and $N$ is odd (so 2 is not a factor).

**Key observation:** The product of numbers each $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ is itself $\equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.

Since $N \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, **at least one** prime factor $q$ of $N$ must satisfy $q \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$.

**But:** $q$ cannot be any $p_i$, because:
$$p_i \mid 4p_1\cdots p_k \quad \text{and} \quad p_i \mid N \implies p_i \mid 1 \quad \text{(impossible)}$$

This **contradicts** our assumption that the list was complete. $\square$

---

### Examples of such primes:
$$3, 7, 11, 19, 23, 31, 43, 47, 59, 67, \ldots$$

This result also follows as a special case of **Dirichlet's theorem**, which guarantees infinitely many primes in any arithmetic progression $a + nd$ where $\gcd(a, d) = 1$ — here $a=3,\ d=4$.
